item.title: Fall Travel Takes Off as Backroads Sees 30 Percent Booking Growth
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Fall is becoming a season of its own for active travelers, with Backroads reporting that reservations for September through November have increased more than 30 percent since 2023. The growth is prompting the active travel company to expand its fall 2026 and 2027 offerings, from leaf-peeping adventures in New England and Quebec to hiking beneath the Northern Lights in Finland, Norway, Sweden and Iceland, along with springtime adventures in Australia and New Zealand. Many itineraries pair outdoor exploration with luxury hotels and smaller-group experiences, taking advantage of milder weather and fewer crowds.

The shift toward shoulder-season travel reflects a broader desire to experience destinations at a more relaxed pace while still enjoying active pursuits. Backroads’ fall lineup includes biking, hiking, walking and multi-adventure trips, as well as private departures, women’s adventures and family-focused itineraries.

The Curated Take: The appeal of fall travel is hardly new, but the growth in active travel suggests travelers are becoming more intentional about when they go, not just where. Cooler temperatures, changing landscapes and fewer visitors can make the shoulder season particularly well suited to travelers who want to experience a destination on foot or by bike rather than simply see it from a resort.

Photo credit: Backroads

item.title: Travelers Rally Behind Nepal Flood Appeal as Donations Near AU$30,000
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Within hours of launching an emergency appeal for communities affected by devastating flooding in Nepal’s Rasuwa district near the Tibet border, the World Expeditions Foundation was approaching its AU$30,000 fundraising target. The response highlights the deep connection many travelers have with Nepal, a country where World Expeditions has operated for decades and built long-standing relationships with local communities, guides and partners. The company has also confirmed that all World Expeditions clients and staff currently traveling in Nepal are safe.

The foundation is directing donations toward communities affected by the flash flood and will continue to share updates as recovery efforts unfold. For travelers who have experienced Nepal firsthand, the appeal offers an opportunity to support communities that have long welcomed visitors to the country’s trekking and mountaineering regions.

The Curated Take: Travel creates connections that often extend well beyond a trip. The rapid response to this appeal is a reminder that the relationship between travelers and destinations can become especially meaningful when communities face a crisis. For those who know Nepal through its landscapes, culture and people, this is a chance to give something back.

Photo credit: World Expeditions Foundation

item.title: Iguassu Falls Reveals a Different Side From the Water
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Iguassu Falls is synonymous with dramatic cascades and lush biodiversity, but some of the most interesting ways to experience the destination begin away from its famous viewpoints. Along the Iguaçu and Paraná rivers, travelers can get closer to the landscape through experiences ranging from the adrenaline of Macuco Safari, which combines jungle, trail and boat excursions before approaching the falls, to more leisurely cruises that reveal the region’s scenery, history and unique position where Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay meet.

For those seeking a slower pace, the approximately one-hour Iguassu River Tour offers sunset views and stories of the bridges and borders connecting the three countries, while the Kattamaram II provides a broader sightseeing experience encompassing the meeting of the Paraná and Iguaçu rivers, the Friendship Bridge and Three Borders Landmark. Together, these experiences offer a fresh perspective on a destination most travelers think they already know.

The Curated Take: Seeing Iguassu Falls from the water changes the scale of the experience. The rivers aren’t simply another activity to add to an itinerary; they reveal how deeply the destination’s geography, wildlife, history and neighboring countries are intertwined. For travelers willing to look beyond the iconic viewpoint, the waterways offer a more expansive way to understand Iguassu.

Photo credit: Visit Iguassu

item.title: Shinta Mani Wild Brings Dental Care to Children in Cambodia’s Cardamom Mountains
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
This September, Shinta Mani Wild will transform a primary school in Cambodia’s remote Cardamom Mountains into a temporary dental clinic, bringing free care and oral health education to hundreds of children who have limited access to professional healthcare. From September 8–14, the luxury conservation camp will host Global Dental Relief and the Shinta Mani Foundation for a seven-day volunteer clinic at Prey Praseth Primary School, providing examinations, fluoride treatments, restorative care and education, alongside a new children’s multivitamin program addressing broader nutritional needs.

The initiative expands a partnership between Global Dental Relief and the Shinta Mani Foundation that has provided dental care to thousands of Cambodian children since 2014. A team of volunteer dentists and clinical support staff will work with local partners to deliver care to an estimated 650–800 children, while the Shinta Mani Wild team supports transportation, translation, meals and logistics. The effort also reflects the camp’s broader conservation philosophy, linking the wellbeing of neighboring communities with the long-term protection of the surrounding rainforest.

The Curated Take: At Shinta Mani Wild, conservation is being approached as something that extends beyond protecting the landscape. Bringing essential healthcare into one of Cambodia’s most remote regions demonstrates how responsible luxury travel can be connected to the wellbeing of the communities that surround protected wilderness. It is a meaningful reminder that the strongest conservation stories often begin with people.

Photo credit: Global Dental Relief

item.title: Seattle Southside Turns Fall Into a Season of Global Flavors and Local Discoveries
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Fall in Seattle Southside brings a distinctly international flavor, led by the newly expanded Global Dining District in SeaTac, formerly the World Table District. Along International Boulevard, locally owned restaurants, cafes and markets invite travelers to taste their way through the region, from Ethiopian coffee and Salvadoran specialties to birria tacos and Peruvian cuisine, while new public art adds another layer to the experience. The district is also set to grow with future international night markets and additional placemaking projects.

The season extends well beyond dining. Des Moines Marina Oktoberfest brings three days of waterfront festivities September 18–20, including an OktoberCrawl and an Oktoberfest Brews Cruise on Puget Sound, while fall itineraries can combine wooded trails, seasonal nursery displays, spa time, farm-to-table dining and the Seattle Chocolate Factory. New openings, including Haidilao Hot Pot, Immersive Gamebox and THE GUNDAM BASE, add even more reasons to explore the region, alongside fall events ranging from bonsai workshops and foliage festivals to Halloween at the Museum of Flight.

The Curated Take: Seattle Southside’s appeal this fall is its sheer variety. Rather than positioning itself simply as an alternative base for visiting Seattle, the region is developing experiences that reflect its own cultural diversity, independent businesses and waterfront communities. The result is a destination where a fall weekend can move effortlessly from global dining to local art, outdoor exploration and a stein overlooking Puget Sound.

Photo credit: Explore Seattle Southside

item.title: Lemala Kuria Hills Reimagines the Safari Stay in Tanzania’s Northern Serengeti
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Lemala Kuria Hills Lodge in Tanzania’s Northern Serengeti has completed a renovation designed to enhance the guest experience without expanding beyond its established wilderness footprint. The refresh introduces a new two-bedroom family suite with generous living space and a private plunge pool, relocates the spa and redesigns and expands the main dining tent. Set among the granite boulders and kopjes of Wogakuria Hill near the Mara River, the lodge remains ideally positioned for the Great Migration while offering year-round wildlife viewing.

The new family suite adds flexibility for multigenerational travelers and groups, while the redesigned dining and spa spaces strengthen the lodge’s connection to its surrounding landscape. Guests can also explore the Northern Serengeti by guided game drive, walking safari or hot-air balloon, with the region’s relatively low visitor density offering a more intimate wilderness experience.

The Curated Take: The renovation is notable for what it does not do. Rather than adding more structures to the landscape, Lemala has reworked its existing footprint to create a more flexible, family-friendly experience while preserving the sense of place that makes a remote Serengeti camp special. For travelers seeking safari with both comfort and a lighter touch on the wilderness, that distinction matters.

Photo credit: Lemala Camps and Lodges

item.title: At Patina Maldives, Guests Help Turn Art Into Part of the Reef
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Patina Maldives, Fari Islands, art is taking a decidedly underwater direction. Through September 12, 2026, the resort is hosting designer and artist Sean Wotherspoon for a collaboration spanning fashion, vintage design and marine conservation, culminating in Respect the Reef, a large-scale ceramic fish sculpture created with resort guests and now submerged in the lagoon as part of Patina’s ongoing coral restoration efforts.

The project brings Wotherspoon’s signature use of color into Patina’s existing ceramic coral workshops. Guests created and glazed individual ceramic scales, which were assembled onto a sculptural fish rather than the geometric structures traditionally used in the resort’s reef program. The completed work has now been placed underwater, where coral can attach and grow across its surface. Above water, Wotherspoon’s creative influence continues through an exclusive capsule collection of original artworks, vintage finds and reworked one-of-one pieces, including Hawaiian shirts and Carhartt shorts, displayed at the Fari Art Atelier.

The Curated Take

The most interesting luxury souvenirs are often the ones that don’t come home with you. At Patina Maldives, guests contribute to something that will remain long after their departure, watching a colorful piece of collaborative art gradually become part of the marine environment. It’s a particularly compelling expression of experiential luxury: the memory is personal, but the creation ultimately belongs to the reef.

Photo Credit: Patina Maldives, Fari Islands

item.title: Hamilton Island Wins Travel Brand of the Year in Australia
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Hamilton Island has been named Travel Brand of the Year – Destination at the 2026 Mumbrella Travel Marketing Awards, recognizing the Australian island’s evolving brand, marketing strategy and creative work. The award follows a period of significant investment, including the debut of The Sundays boutique hotel, a refreshed dining scene featuring Catseye Pool Club by Josh and Julie Niland, and updates to longtime island favorites. In August 2025, Hamilton Island also launched A Little Island Can Do Wonders, its first major brand campaign since 2017, inviting travelers to rediscover the Whitsundays destination.

At the heart of the island’s latest chapter is a broader evolution of the guest experience, from its 20 restaurants and extensive activities to its access to Whitehaven Beach and the Great Barrier Reef. With 70 percent of the island protected, Hamilton Island combines resort amenities with opportunities to explore the surrounding landscape, while recent accolades for properties including qualia and The Sundays add to its growing international profile.

The Curated Take: The award is less about a single campaign than what Hamilton Island has built around it. The destination is using new hospitality, dining and experiences to give travelers a fresh reason to return, while its latest branding connects that evolution back to the simple appeal of an island escape. It is a useful reminder that a strong destination brand has to keep giving travelers something new to discover.

Photo credit: Hamilton Island

item.title: Scottsdale’s Culinary Scene Earns Five Michelin Guide Southwest Honors
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Scottsdale is making a notable showing in the inaugural MICHELIN Guide Southwest, with five restaurants recognized in the guide’s first selection covering Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico and Utah. FnB earned a Bib Gourmand for chef Charleen Badman’s seasonally driven celebration of Arizona farmers and producers, while Hush Public House, Indibar, Reserve and Shinbay received Michelin Recommended honors. Reserve’s wine director, John Germain, also received a Sommelier Award, while Badman was recognized with a Mindful Voices Award for her work advancing sustainability and food access through the Blue Watermelon Project.

The selection follows Michelin’s expansion into the Southwest and its evaluation of restaurants based on quality of ingredients, harmony of flavors, cooking technique, culinary personality and consistency. For travelers, the recognition puts Scottsdale’s increasingly diverse dining scene firmly on the culinary map, highlighting everything from Arizona-focused cooking and Indian cuisine to Japanese omakase and sophisticated wine programs.

The Curated Take: Michelin’s inaugural Southwest guide gives travelers another reason to put Scottsdale on the itinerary. More importantly, the range of honors shows a destination dining scene that goes well beyond resort restaurants, with local ingredients, global influences and chefs who are putting their own stamp on the Southwest.

Photo credit: Experience Scottsdale and Jill Richards Photography

item.title: Coastal Mississippi’s Fall Calendar Turns Milestones Into Reasons to Visit
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
From live blues and songwriter sessions to classic cars, catamaran racing, art festivals and Gulf Coast seafood, Coastal Mississippi is heading into fall with a calendar that is as diverse as its 62 miles of shoreline. Beginning Labor Day weekend and continuing through November, the destination’s biggest events combine long-running local traditions with milestone celebrations that give travelers plenty of reasons to plan a coastal escape.

The season begins with the 7th Annual Booker Fest in Bay St. Louis and Artwalk Downtown Ocean Springs over Labor Day weekend, followed by the Biloxi Box Set Music Festival, Biloxi Seafood Festival and 35th Annual Gulf Coast Blues Festival. September also brings the Hobie 16 International Championship, drawing top catamaran sailors from around the world, and the Mississippi Songwriters Festival, where roughly 200 singer-songwriters will perform across Ocean Springs and Gautier. Later in the month, Banana Ball brings its deliberately unpredictable brand of baseball to Biloxi.

October shifts the spotlight to one of Coastal Mississippi’s biggest traditions, as Cruisin’ the Coast celebrates its 30th anniversary with more than 10,000 classic, antique and hot rod vehicles traveling along Highway 90. The fall calendar continues with the 40th Annual Fall Muster, the 10th Annual Gulf Coast Equality Fest and the century-plus Jackson County Blue Ribbon Fair. November brings the 48th annual Peter Anderson Arts & Crafts Festival in Ocean Springs, followed by Bud & Burgers in the Bay and the Scottish Highland Games and Celtic Music Festival.

The Curated Take: The appeal of Coastal Mississippi in fall isn’t simply that there is something happening every weekend. It’s that the events reveal the character of the destination. Music reflects its Southern and Gulf Coast roots, Cruisin’ the Coast turns the shoreline into a moving celebration, art festivals showcase local creativity, and sailing puts the region’s waterways center stage. For travelers, the calendar offers an easy reason to choose a particular weekend and then build a broader coastal getaway around it.

Photo credit: Coastal Mississippi / Visit Mississippi
